questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: McGill Law was an obvious choice due to its strong international reputation and its unique transsystemic approach, which offered exposure to both civil law and common law traditions. The Faculty’s particular strengths in international law, human rights, and trade law closely aligned with my academic focus and complemented my legal training at the University of Copenhagen. In addition, studying in Montreal provided an intellectually vibrant, bilingual environment that encouraged comparative and interdisciplinary thinking, which was a key motivation for choosing my study destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Overall, it was relatively easy to find the necessary information upon arrival. McGill provided clear pre-arrival guidance, and key practical information regarding registration, course selection, and academic expectations was well structured and accessible online. Any remaining questions were easily resolved through orientation activities and responsive support from administrative staff, which made the transition smooth.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Upon arrival, I received structured support through orientation activities and introductory sessions organized by the university and the Faculty of Law. These provided practical guidance on academic procedures, course registration, and campus resources. In addition, administrative staff were accessible and helpful in addressing individual questions, which ensured a smooth start to the exchange period.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Future exchange students should be aware that living off campus in Montreal is very common and generally affordable, but it requires early planning. Popular neighborhoods close to McGill fill up quickly, and leases often start on fixed dates, so flexibility is important. While public transport is reliable and makes commuting easy, students should factor in winter conditions when choosing location and housing quality. Overall, off-campus living offers independence and a good integration into local life, but it rewards those who plan ahead.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process at the host institution was well organized and largely straightforward. Course selection and enrollment were conducted online prior to the semester, with clear guidance provided by the Faculty of Law. Any adjustments after arrival were handled efficiently, and support from academic advisors and administrative staff made it easy to resolve scheduling or enrollment issues.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Support was available through orientation sessions, academic advising, and responsive administrative staff at the Faculty of Law. In addition, central student services provided assistance with practical matters such as registration, housing guidance, and access to campus resources, which made it easy to obtain help when needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all my courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Future exchange students should familiarize themselves with the online registration system well in advance and carefully review course descriptions and prerequisites before enrolling. It is advisable to have a prioritized list of alternative courses, as popular classes can fill up quickly. Making use of the add/drop period and staying in contact with academic advisors can help resolve any scheduling issues efficiently.

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses was demanding and appropriate for advanced law students. Classes required a high degree of preparation, including extensive reading and active participation, and assessments emphasized analytical skills rather than memorization. Overall, the academic level was comparable to upper-level Master’s courses and provided a strong intellectual challenge.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style at the host institution was more interactive and discussion-based than at UCPH. Classes placed greater emphasis on student participation, case analysis, and continuous engagement throughout the semester, whereas teaching at UCPH is generally more lecture-oriented and exam-focused. This difference encouraged more active preparation and ongoing reflection, and it complemented my academic experience well.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Some unexpected costs included higher-than-anticipated expenses related to housing deposits, winter-related clothing and utilities, and course materials. In addition, everyday costs such as groceries and public transportation were slightly higher than expected, particularly over the winter months. Overall, these costs were manageable but worth budgeting for in advance.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend joining non-academic activities such as swimming, a book club, and a choir. These activities provide a good balance to academic work, offer structured breaks from studying, and make it easy to meet people outside the law faculty. They also help create a sense of routine and community, which greatly enhances the overall exchange experience.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the Rocky mountains. Explore the rest of Quebec: Go see blue whales in Tadoussac and go on hikes with random people. Go to the MOC house. Maybe a weekend in Boston or New York. But dont support the US unnecessarily. Go to concerts. Go to sport events. Go the the cinema. Enjoy your life. Spend some time on the mountain as well. Talk to people.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the local culture was relatively easy. Montreal is an open and internationally oriented city, and the bilingual environment made it welcoming for exchange students. Cultural differences were present but easy to navigate, and the inclusive academic and social atmosphere at the university facilitated a smooth adjustment.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: NO. Do it in you own way and in your own tempo.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There were no major cultural differences that were particularly challenging. However, adapting to a more informal classroom culture with higher expectations of continuous participation required some adjustment. Additionally, the bilingual context occasionally created minor practical challenges, but overall these differences were easy to navigate.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I particularly appreciated the openness and inclusivity of the local culture, as well as the strong emphasis on community and dialogue both inside and outside the classroom. The bilingual and international environment encouraged curiosity and exchange of perspectives, and the city’s vibrant cultural life made it easy to feel engaged beyond academics. Whatsoever, I did not like when Montreal became to American.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Plan your courses early. Familiarize yourself with the registration system and have backup options, as popular courses fill up quickly.
Be prepared for active participation. Classes are discussion-based and require continuous engagement and thorough preparation.
Embrace life off campus. Living off campus and joining non-academic activities is a great way to integrate into local life and get the most out of the exchange experience.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Future exchange students may benefit from knowing that the academic workload is continuous rather than concentrated around a final exam, so steady preparation is important. It is also useful to plan housing and administrative matters early, as timelines and procedures may differ from those at UCPH. Finally, taking advantage of orientation activities and student organizations can greatly enhance both the academic and social aspects of the exchange.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It was the break I needed from Denmark. Also, you get some perspectives on your life at home that are essentail for your further movement. I am not a whole new person. But close.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All the time on my own with my own thoughts and all my freetime without substantial stuff to do. Either you will find out that it is not that bad. Otherwise you will go insane.
